# Dendrimer nanotherapy targeting of glial dysfunction improves inflammation and neurobehavioral phenotype in adult female Mecp2-heterozygous mouse model of Rett syndrome

**Authors:** Elizabeth Smith Khoury; Ruchit V. Patel; Caroline O’Ferrall; Amanda Fowler; Nirnath Sah; Anjali Sharma; Siddharth Gupta; Susanna Scafidi; Josh Kurtz; Sarah J. Olmstead; Sapna R. Kudchadkar; Rangaramanujam M. Kannan; Mary E. Blue; Sujatha Kannan

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Anesthesiology and Critical Care Medicine, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Baltimore, MD | 2Center for Nanomedicine, Department of Ophthalmology, Wilmer Eye Institute, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Baltimore, MD | 3Departments of Pediatrics and Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Baltimore, MD | 4Department of Neurology, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Baltimore MD, 21205 | 5Department of Neuroscience, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Baltimore MD, 21205 | 6Hugo W. Moser Research Institute at Kennedy Krieger Inc., Baltimore MD, 21205 | 7Kennedy Krieger Institute – Johns Hopkins University for Cerebral Palsy Research Excellence, Baltimore, MD 21287 | 8Departments of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering, and Materials Science and Engineering, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore MD, 21218 | 9Kennedy Krieger Institute, Department of Neurology, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Baltimore, MD 21287

## Abstract

Rett syndrome is an X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder caused by mutation of Mecp2 gene and primarily affects females. Glial cell dysfunction has been implicated in in Rett syndrome (RTT) both in patients and in mouse models of this disorder and can affect synaptogenesis, glial metabolism and inflammation. Here we assessed whether treatment of adult (5–6 months old) symptomatic Mecp2-heterozygous female mice with N-acetyl cysteine conjugated to dendrimer (D-NAC), which is known to target glia and modulate inflammation and oxidative injury, results in improved behavioral phenotype, sleep and glial inflammatory profile. We show that unbiased global metabolomic analysis of the hippocampus and striatum in adult Mecp2-heterozygous mice demonstrates significant differences in lipid metabolism associated with neuroinflammation, providing the rationale for targeting glial inflammation in this model. Our results demonstrate that treatment with D-NAC (10 mg/kg NAC) once weekly is more efficacious than equivalently dosed free NAC in improving the gross neurobehavioral phenotype in symptomatic Mecp2-heterozygous female mice. We also show that D-NAC therapy is significantly better than saline in ameliorating several aspects of the abnormal phenotype including paw clench, mobility, fear memory, REM sleep and epileptiform activity burden. Systemic D-NAC significantly improves microglial proinflammatory cytokine production and is associated with improvements in several aspects of the phenotype including paw clench, mobility, fear memory, and REM sleep, and epileptiform activity burden in comparison to saline-treated Mecp2-hetereozygous mice. Systemic glial-targeted delivery of D-NAC after symptom onset in an older clinically relevant Rett syndrome model shows promise in improving neurobehavioral impairments along with sleep pattern and epileptiform activity burden. These findings argue for the translational value of this approach for treatment of patients with Rett Syndrome.

## Abstract

Rett syndrome is a neurodevelopmental disorder primarily affecting females, caused by mutations in the Mecp2 gene. Glial cell dysfunction and inflammation contribute to the pathogenesis of this disorder. In this study, we investigated the therapeutic potential of a targeted treatment, N-acetyl cysteine conjugated to dendrimer (D-NAC), in symptomatic Mecp2-heterozygous female mice. We found that D-NAC treatment significantly improved the neurobehavioral phenotype, memory, sleep patterns, and microglial inflammatory profile. This study offers valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms and therapeutic approaches for Rett syndrome, with implications for the development of novel interventions for patients affected by this debilitating condition.

## Introduction

Rett syndrome (RTT) is a severe neurological disorder caused by mutations in the X-chromosome gene MECP2, which encodes the ubiquitous transcription regulator Methyl-CpG-binding-protein 2(Guy et al. 2001; Amir et al. 1999). Patients commonly experience motor impairment, cognitive disabilities, respiratory abnormalities, sleep dysfunction, and epileptiform activities(Neul et al. 2010). Existing treatments do not target the underlying neuropathology and often are only partially effective in symptom mitigation. Notably apneas, sleep disorders (increased night waking, decreased sleep efficiency) and in some cases, seizure activity are not easily managed pharmacologically(McArthur & Budden 1998; Johnston et al. 2014; Chapleau et al. 2013). Mecp2 mutant mice recapitulate features of Rett syndrome observed clinically: mice display abnormal locomotion, cognitive deficits and reduced volumes in hippocampi and striatum – areas of the brain responsible for these deficits (Stearns et al. 2007).

Elevations in serum oxidative stress markers and inflammatory cytokines are observed in patients with RTT, and the magnitude of oxidative stress and inflammation correlate with clinical severity scores in these patients(De Felice et al. 2009; Leoncini et al. 2015). Mouse models of RTT further reveal immune dysregulation and oxidative stress in the brain(Pecorelli et al. 2016). Through these animal models, the role of glia in the production of the neurobehavioral phenotype of RTT has come to be appreciated. Microglia and astrocytes show increased activation and dysregulation leading to elevated inflammation, oxidative stress, and extracellular glutamate in the brains of Mecp2-deficient mice(Kahanovitch et al. 2019). In vivo and in vitro interventions that modulate glial function have had positive effects on key neuropathology and neurobehavioral phenotypes(Horiuchi et al. 2017; Maezawa & Jin 2010; Jin et al. 2015; Nance et al. 2017).These encouraging results suggest a potential therapeutic utility in targeting glia.

We have previously demonstrated that generation 4 (G4) hydroxyl-terminated poly(amidoamine) dendrimers (G4 PAMAM-OH; 4nm, neutral in charge) are taken up specifically by activated glia using a mechanism that takes advantage of its transport across the impaired BBB, rapid diffusion in the brain parenchyma and enhanced fluid phase endocytosis of activated glia compared to other cells(Smith et al. 2019a; Nance et al. 2016; Zhang et al. 2016). N-acetyl cysteine (NAC) when specifically delivered to activated glial cells using dendrimers, decreases inflammation and oxidative stress in diseased brains, resulting in dramatic improvements in neurological outcome in several models of brain injury (Smith et al. 2019a; Alnasser et al. 2018). D-NAC has also shown promise in a Phase 2a clinical trial with improvement in survival and neurologic injury biomarkers in patients with severe COVID (Gusdon et al. 2022). Dendrimer-mediated delivery of NAC also avoids the increased extracellular glutamate production seen with free NAC by bypassing the cysteine-glutamate antiporter (xCT) and avoiding the glutamate toxicity seen with repeated NAC delivery(Nance et al. 2017).

In a Mecp2-null mouse model of RTT, dendrimers are primarily taken up by microglia in the MeCP2-deficient brain, both before and after onset of disease phenotype (Nance et al. 2017). D-NAC treatment starting at 3 weeks of age in this model slowed the progression of the phenotype, while decreasing the toxicity associated with repeated NAC administration(Nance et al. 2017). Here, we assessed the ability of D-NAC to reduce oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and comprehensive disease phenotype (including motor, sleep, epileptiform activity, and cognitive features) in symptomatic female Mecp2-heterozyous (het) mice, which is a more clinically and translationally relevant model. Clinical translation of therapies in RTT have been hindered due in part to the type of preclinical model used. Here we use a model identified by the RTT research community to have better genotypic and phenotypic fidelity to patients with RTT - including larger variability in phenotypic severity(Katz et al. 2012). We show that D-NAC administration improves paw clench severity, mobility, fear memory, and perhaps more importantly sleep and epileptiform activity burden in Mecp2-het mice. These improvements are associated with decreased proinflammatory cytokine production in CD11b+ microglial cells indicating that dendrimer-delivered NAC shows promise for the remediation of both neuropathology and symptoms in patients.

## Materials and Methods

### Animals

Mecp2tm1.1Bird−/+ (heterozygous, het) female mice (Jackson Laboratories, RRID:IMSR_JAX:003890) were bred with wild-type (WT) male mice (all on C57BL/6 background). Mecp2−/+ mice for these experiments were used once they reached 5–6 months of age and were screened for consistent presence behavioral phenotype (abnormal locomotion, paw clench). Mecp2-het mice were also crossed with CX3CR1GFP/GFP male mice (Jackson Laboratories, RRID:IMSR_JAX:005582). Resulting Mecp2-het CX3CR1GFP/+ offspring were aged until 6 months old and then utilized for the dendrimer localization study. Mice were housed 5 per cage in a vivarium with a light cycle of 14 hours on and 10 hours off and were allowed free access to food and water. Animals were monitored daily for any signs of distress and evidence of poor or deteriorating health would lead to early euthanasia after consulting with the staff veterinarian. All protocols and procedures were approved by the Johns Hopkins Animal Care and Use Committee (MO18M210; MO21M208) and followed NIH ARRIVE guidelines. At the end of the experiments, animals were killed with pentobarbital 400mg/kg administered IP. The study design was not pre-registered or published online previously. Total number of animals used in the study were 128 (87 Mecp2-het and 41 WT).

#### Metabolomics measurements and profiling.

Unbiased global metabolomics were performed on rapidly dissected and frozen (in liquid nitrogen) striatum and hippocampi from 5–6 months old female wild type mice (controls) and Mecp2−/+ mice (n=5 mice /group). Using liquid chromatography/tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC/MS/MS) platform, multiple classes of metabolites were screened and identified.

#### D-Cy5 localization in Mecp2-het brain.

Dendrimer-Cy5 was synthesized as previously described (Sharma et al. 2018a). Mecp2−/+ Cx3cr1GFP/+ mouse was administered with D-Cy5 intraperitoneally, followed by brain perfusion with phosphate buffer saline after 24 hours. The perfused brain was fixed overnight with buffered 10% formalin and subsequently submerged in 30% sucrose buffer solution for cryoprotection. 30 μm thick coronal brain sections containing the hippocampus were treated with 3% H2O2 followed by DAPI. Confocal images were acquired from the mounted sections using Zeiss ZEN LSM 880 microscope (Zeiss, CA, USA) and image j software (National Institutes of Health) was used for subsequent image processing.

### Synthesis and Characterization of D-NAC

NAC was conjugated to the hydroxyl dendrimer, purified, and confirmed for payload according to previously established protocols(Sharma et al. 2018b). Briefly, each dendrimer was configured to have 22 ± 3 molecules of NAC. NAC was conjugated to the dendrimer with a disulfide bond designed to be cleaved by intracellular concentrations of GSH, confirmed in previous characterization studies(Sharma et al. 2018b).

### Treatment and Assessment Paradigm

Since Rett syndrome typically affects females, in all our experiments we used female Mecp2-het mice, which were randomly assigned using a 4-animal block randomization to 4 experimental groups treated weekly with 1) phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), or 2) empty G4 PAMAM-OH dendrimer (55 mg/kg; equivalent to the amount of dendrimer used to deliver NAC), 3) free NAC (10 mg/kg), or 4) D-NAC (10 mg/kg on a NAC basis), dissolved in PBS. Animals were numbered and sequentially assigned to one of the 4 treatment groups. Injections were administered intraperitoneally (i.p.) in a volume of 20 μl, and all formulations were in sterile PBS. Drug assignments and injections were performed by experimenters who were not involved with any of the assessments or analysis. WT mice (controls) were injected weekly with PBS. A weekly treatment interval was chosen as we have previously shown that dendrimers can reside in tissue for up to 9 days (Nance et al. 2016). Behavioral assessments were started 72 hours after the third dose injection. The order of behavioral testing was: neurobehavioral scores and open field followed by contextual fear conditioning (Week 3). Assessments were done in cohorts of litter mates. Since contextual fear conditioning is a more stressful test it was the final assessment done. Sleep and epileptiform activity assessments using untethered EEG recordings in the home cage were conducted in a separate set of mice injected weekly for 3 weeks prior to recording.

### Neurobehavioral Scoring

A previously established neurobehavioral score (analogous to the RTT clinical severity score) was used to assess gross neurobehavioral phenotype. The scoring system has 6 sub-scores, one for each of the following: gait, mobility, paw clench (back left paw), paw clench (back right paw), and respiration (all scored on a scale of 0–3, where 0 is normal and 3 is severely impaired). All Mecp2-het mice required a baseline score ≥ 2, including a paw clench score of > 0, to be included in the behavioral experiment. An experimenter who was blinded to the treatment scored neurobehavioral testing videos, and test days scores were compared to baseline scores (prior to treatment).

### Open Field

Mice were allowed to move freely in an enclosure (38 cm × 26.5 cm) for 10 minutes. Ethovision tracking software (version 11; Noldus) was used to quantify distance traveled, velocity of horizontal movement, and time spent in the center of the open field. Rearing behavior was hand scored by an experimenter blinded to treatment group. The enclosure was cleaned with 70% ethanol between each trial.

### Contextual Fear Conditioning

On Day 1, mice were placed in the fear conditioning chamber (10.75” × 9.97” × 11.25”; MedAssociates, VT). After 2 minutes of habituation, mice were exposed to three tone–shock pairings delivered 2 minutes apart. Each tone was 30 seconds in duration, and the 2-second shock (0.7 mV) co-terminated with the tone. On Day 2, mice were placed back into the chamber (Context A) for 5 minutes. One hour later, mice were placed into a novel context (Context B, flat floor, visual cues, scent changed). In Context B, the mice experienced 2 minutes of habituation and then three tone-only presentations at 1-minute intervals. All sessions were video recorded and analyzed with AnyMaze Software. Assessments were done by an experimenter who was blinded to the treatment.

### Microglial Cytokine Analyses

Mecp2-het mice were treated with either saline or D-NAC (10 mg/kg on a NAC basis) weekly for 4 weeks. Brains were extracted 24 hours after the last injection, and cells were obtained with the adult brain dissociation kit and protocol (Miltenyi, Cat. No. 130–107-677). After completion of this protocol, myelin was removed by using myelin beads. A CD11b-bead was then used to positively select for microglia via magnetic sorting (CD11b+ beads, Miltenyi Cat. No. 130049601). CD11b+ cells were eluted from the column, and protein was extracted from these cells to assess cytokine presence. The Proinflammatory Panel 1 from Mesoscale Diagnostics (Cat. No. K15048D, Rockville, MD) was utilized for this experiment. The manufacturer’s protocol and reagents were used for all steps. For each sample, 50 µg of protein was used per well. Briefly, samples and standards were incubated overnight, detection antibody was incubated for 2 hours, and the plate was read after addition of 2× read buffer (Mesoscale Discovery, Mesoscale QuickPlex SQ 120). Data were analyzed with the associated Workbench software.

### EEG Surgery

Mice were anesthetized in a chamber with inhaled 4% isoflurane and were maintained on 2–3% isoflurane through a nose cone (flow rate = 2 L/min). This is well tolerated by the Het mice with good recovery. A heating pad (37°C) was placed under the stereotaxic operating setup to maintain body temperature. A wireless EEG transmitter implant (Data Sciences International, HD-X02) was placed dorsally in a subcutaneous pocket. Electromyography (EMG) lead wires were secured in the cervical trapezius muscles. A micro-drill was then used to perforate the skull. Two monopolar EEG lead wires were inserted to make electrical contact with the dura (one per burr hole) and secured with dental cement on the surface of the brain at 1mm anterior to bregma and 1–2mm lateral from the midline. One (placed at 3mm posterior to bregma and 1–2mm lateral to the midline on the same hemisphere) was used as a reference electrode. Mice recovered for 3 days prior to initiation of recording.

### EEG/EMG Recording

A separate group of mice were single housed in their home cage on top of the telemetry receiver pads for EEG/EMG signal capture (Data Sciences International, PhysioTel Receiver RPC-1). Mice were recorded with Ponemah Software (Data Sciences International, Version 6.40) for 72 hours on a light-dark cycle matching that of their vivarium environment. The EEG/EMG signal was sampled at 500 Hz.

### EEG Analyses

The EEG/EMG/video recording was imported into Neuroscore Software (Data Sciences International, Version 3.2.1). The first 24 hours of each recording (Day 1) were not included in the analysis. EEG data for Days 2 and 3 were then scored using Neuroscore (epoch length = 10 seconds) using previously established methods for vigilance state assignment and state transition identification (Olivadoti & Opp 2008; Tang & Sanford 2002; Wisor et al. 2011). The four vigilance states assigned were active wake (AW), quiet wake (QW), non-rapid eye movement sleep (NREM), and rapid eye movement sleep (REM). EEG signal was subjected to fast Fourier transformation (FFT) and power bands were assigned. Delta was defined as 1–4 Hz and Theta as 6–9 Hz. These spectra were computed for EEG signal every 2s and averaged for each 10s epoch. Scoring criteria for each vigilance state were based on EEG signal and delta/theta frequency, EMG signal, and visual inspection of mouse on video feed. Briefly, definitions for each vigilance state were as follows: AW – high amplitude/high frequency EEG (i.e. mixed theta and delta frequency), high amplitude EMG, purposeful movements visible; QW – high amplitude/high frequency EEG (i.e. mixed theta and delta frequency), low amplitude EMG, no purposeful movements visible; NREM – high amplitude/low frequency EEG (i.e. delta > theta frequency), low amplitude EMG, no movements visible; REM – low amplitude/high frequency synchronous EEG (i.e. theta > delta frequency), very low amplitude EMG, no movements visible. Data across Days 2 and 3 were averaged prior to statistical analyses.

#### Epileptiform activity detection

24-hour long EEG voltage traces were analyzed using a previously established spike train detection module (Bastlund et al. 2004; Weiergräber et al. 2008). Epileptiform discharges were defined as spike trains consisting of ≥ 3 spikes with an amplitude of at least 1.5-fold of the baseline electrical activity, and frequencies between 6 and 10 Hz (Wither et al. 2018; Purtell et al. 2018). Furthermore, EEG traces were visually inspected and analyzed by a blinded reviewer to determine the incidences of epileptiform discharges.

### Statistics

All statistical analyses were performed using Graphpad Prism Software (version 8). We did not utilize statistical methods to determine the sample size in advance; however, our sample sizes are similar to those documented in previous publications (Nance et al. 2017; Khoury et al. 2020). Data were analyzed by one-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s post hoc tests. If homogeneity of variance was violated, a Brown-Forsythe test was used. Two-way ANOVA was used in analyses of longitudinal behavioral data. Statistical significance was set at p = 0.05. Improvement in neurobehavioral score, fear memory and sleep structure with D-NAC treatment in Mecp2-het mice were primary outcomes with microglial inflammatory cytokine expression as secondary outcome and epileptiform discharges as exploratory outcome. The JHU Anesthesiology & Critical Care Medicine Biostatistics Core provided statistical support for analysis.

## Results

### Adult female Mecp2-het brain display specific metabolic profile.

We performed an unbiased global metabolome analysis of dissected striatum and hippocampi from WT (controls) and Mecp2−/+ mice and determined the relative abundances of 591 metabolites. Principal component analysis of metabolite summary show that WT (controls) and Mecp2−/+ mice cluster within their specific genotype groups (Figure 1a). Further analyses revealed that significant metabolic differences were detected between these two groups. Specifically, in hippocampi of Mecp2−/+ mice 42 metabolites were significantly increased, and 11 significantly decreased compared to WT controls. In the striatum of Mecp2−/+ mice, 70 metabolites were significantly increased and 23 significantly decreased when compared to WT controls. The starkest differences were observed in lipid metabolism pathway. Specifically, both hippocampi and striatum of Mecp2−/+ mice demonstrated increased long-chain fatty acids metabolites, phospholipids and lysolipids depending on the molecular species (Figure 1b,c & d, and Supplement Tables 1-3 for related statistical report). Surprisingly, striatum of Mecp2−/+ mice showed significant accumulation of sphingolipids and sphingosines compared to their WT controls and recapitulate perturbations on sphingolipid metabolism observed clinically in females with Rett syndrome (Cappuccio et al., Metabolites, 2019). Significant increase in sphingolipids were detected in the stratum and hippocampi of Mecp2−/+, which are affected in RTT pathology and participate in regulation of inflammatory pathways, provided the rationale for targeting glial inflammation as a therapeutic strategy in this model. In addition, perturbations in metabolites linked to neurotransmission, transsulfuration and NAD pathway were noted in the hippocampus and striatum of Mecp2−/+ mice (see supplement Figure. S1).

### Dendrimer nanoparticles are taken up into glia of the Mecp2-het brain.

Phenotype-expressing Mecp2-het mice were injected with D-Cy5 (55mg/kg) and brains were collected 24 hours later. Microglia in the Mecp2-het brain show uptake of dendrimer in various regions including hippocampus (Figure 2).

### D-NAC Reduces Neurobehavioral Phenotype More Effectively Than Free NAC

Mice were randomly assigned to 4 different groups and were dosed weekly with either 1) PBS (saline), 2) empty dendrimer (55mg/kg), 3) D-NAC (10mg/kg on a NAC basis equivalent to 55mg/kg dendrimer basis), or 4) NAC (10mg/kg). Mecp2-het mice treated with either PBS (HET + Saline), empty dendrimer (HET + dendrimer), or NAC (HET + NAC) demonstrated significantly abnormal high score (analogous to the clinical severity score) compared to WT (control) mice (Fig. 3A). In contrast, D-NAC-treated Mecp2-het mice showed improved total neurobehavior score, and specifically paw clench severity. (Figure 3a, b). D-NAC-treated Mecp2-het mice also showed 50% more horizontal movement/exploratory behavior than did saline-treated mice (Figure 3c) but exhibited no improvement in time spent in center or in rearing behavior (Figure 3d, e). Since Mecp2-het mice did not show any improvement with free NAC treatment, the free NAC group was removed from subsequent behavioral experiments.

### Systemic D-NAC therapy improved Fear Memory

MeCP2-deficiency is known to result in deficits of learning and memory, specifically fear memory, due to aberrant functional neural circuitry in the hippocampus and amygdala(Smith et al. 2019b). Mecp2-het mice exhibited no impairment in freezing in the familiar context (Context A; Figure 4b, c) or to the initially novel context (Context B; habituation period, Figure 4d). However, when exposed to tones in the novel context (Context B), Mecp2-het mice spent less time freezing than WT; D-NAC treatment rescued this response (Figure 4e). This finding suggests a recovery of cue-dependent memory with D-NAC treatment in Mecp2-het mice.

### Mecp2-het Mice Display Disordered Sleep/Wake States, which is rescued by D-NAC therapy

Mecp2-het mice showed altered sleep states with less total sleep time than WT mice (Figure 5a). The global reduction of sleep in Mecp2-het mice was a result of less time spent in both paradoxical sleep (PS)/REM slow-and wave sleep/NREM compared to WT counterparts (Figure 5b, c). D-NAC treatment in Mecp2-het mice had the greatest effect on rescuing REM time (Figure 5b, d, g) but did not recover total sleep time or NREM time within the relatively short treatment duration of 3 weeks (Figure 5a, c). Additionally, the global recovery of REM sleep time was driven by a 50% increase in light phase REM time only (Figure 5d). When we examined parameters of REM sleep in the light phase, Mecp2-het mice had shorter REM bouts with decreased REM mean length that recovers to WT levels after DNAC treatment (Figure 5e). Globally, there was no effect of genotype on sleep-wake transitions (Figure 5f). However, when examining REM-to-wake transitions specifically, Mecp2-het mice showed a significant increase in the rate of REM-to-wake state transitions when compared to their WT counterparts (Figure 5g) D-NAC treatment reduced the rate of REM-to-wake state transitions by approximately 40% in Mecp2-het mice to that seen in WT mice (Figure 5g).

### Systemic D-NAC decreases epileptiform activity burden

The presence and count of epileptiform activity varied widely among Mecp2-het mice (Figure 6). Wild type mice did not show any epileptiform activityMecp2-het mice exhibited intense epileptiform activity, whereas all the D-NAC-treated Mecp2-het mice had significantly less epileptiform activity counts (Figure 6b) and epileptiform activity duration (Figure 6c) (p < 0.05).

### Systemically delivered D-NAC decreases inflammatory cytokines in microglia

Cytokine assessment of CD11b+ microglia demonstrated a significant increase in TNF-α and IL-1β expression in the microglia isolated from Mecp2-het mice as compared to WT mice. D-NAC therapy resulted in a ~70% reduction in IL-1β and a trend in reduction of TNF-α. (Figure 7).

## Discussion

Our results show that systemic nanoparticle-targeted therapy is effective in mitigating glial-related pathology in a clinically relevant, symptomatic Mecp2-het mouse model of RTT. Weekly D-NAC therapy at 10 mg/kg on a NAC basis decreases proinflammatory cytokine production in Mecp2-het mice. These effects correspond with reduction of behavioral phenotype, as treated Mecp2-het mice show a decrease in neurobehavioral phenotype severity, increase in mobility, and improvements in fear memory, REM sleep, and epileptiform activity burden. Notably, this is the first study to demonstrate that glial-targeted therapeutic interventions can mitigate phenotype of female heterozygous mice. We also show for the first time that adult female Mecp2-het mice demonstrate significant perturbations in lipid metabolism in the areas of the brain which control behaviors observed in these mice. While glycolysis and tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediates remained largely unchanged, we detected significant perturbation in lipid metabolism in both the hippocampus and striatum of Mecp2−/+ mice. Specifically, we observed significant changes in sphingolipids, which have rapid turnover and major regulators of inflammation (Maceyka & Spiegel 2014) and in acylcarnitines in the striatum that have been shown to be pro-inflammatory (Rutkowsky et al. 2014). Sphingolipids may be both anti-inflammatory and pro-inflammatory and have been reported to participate in TNF-α signaling (Maceyka & Spiegel 2014). This is in contrast to what was previously published for 50 day old Mecp2 null male mice where metabolomic analysis in the cortex showed primarily changes in carbohydrate metabolism and tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediates (Golubiani et al. 2021). These differences may be related to the age, genotype, sex and brain regions evaluated.

Importantly, there are no neurobehavioral improvements seen with the same dose of NAC delivered freely. Previously, free NAC was not effective in improving the behavioral phenotype in Mecp2-null mice and resulted in toxicity, likely from increased glutamate release extracellularly via xCT (Nance et al., 2017). The efficacy of D-NAC on behavioral phenotype is seen with doses that are 5–15 fold lower and less frequent than what was observed for free NAC in other models of neuroinflammation (Cao et al., 2012; Rahimmi et al., 2015). Enhancement in the therapeutic effect of NAC with dendrimer-mediated delivery can be explained by: 1) the dendrimer facilitates uptake into target cell populations, with D-NAC localizing in activated glia, 2) dendrimer-conjugation with a disulfide linker protects NAC from being cleaved until it is exposed to intracellular GSH conditions (Navath et al. 2010), 3) D-NAC circumvents potential toxicities previously seen with repeated NAC dosing (Nance et al, 2017). Mecp2-null mice have increased expression of cysteine-glutamate antiporter (system xc-), one of the main mechanisms of cysteine uptake into the cell (for subsequent GSH formation) that results in increased glutamate release extracellularly (Nance et al., 2017). NAC can increase extracellular glutamate levels (Bridges et al., 2012) which would be deleterious in RTT, while DNAC bypasses system xc- .

Loss of Mecp2 in both Mecp2-null and Mecp2-het mice compromises innate functionality of microglia and their response to inflammatory or other cell stressors (e.g. hypoxia)(Cronk et al. 2015; Zhao et al. 2017). Immune response genes are more prominently dysregulated in later phenotypic stages in both Mecp2-null males and Mecp2-het females(Cronk et al. 2015; Zhao et al. 2017). This finding suggests that microglial dysfunction is a dynamic process, likely influenced by both neural development and the presence of additional pathologies. Data from patients with RTT support this possibility, and inflammation and oxidative stress are tightly linked to disease progression and clinical severity (Leoncini et al. 2015; Pecorelli et al. 2016; Valacchi et al. 2017).

D-NAC reduced gross neurobehavioral phenotype score, most prominently stereotypic paw clench in adult Mecp2-het mice. Paw clenching is the predominant sub score present in these mice and is analogous to stereotypic hand movements commonly observed in RTT(Amir et al. 1999). Open field mobility in Mecp2-het mice also improved with D-NAC, but not free NAC administration. This aligns with our previous findings that free NAC was ineffective in improving Mecp2-null phenotype(Nance et al. 2017). Previously, oxidative stress and phenotype have been correlated, and our current work provides evidence for a causal relationship between glial dysfunction and the behavioral phenotype seen in Mecp2-deficient mice(Pecorelli et al. 2016; Valacchi et al. 2017). Because D-NAC showed better efficacy in this experiment as compared to free NAC, we exclusively studied D-NAC in subsequent experiments to further vet this technology for its translational value.

We found that inflammation contributes to the production of fear memory deficits in Mecp2-het mice—deficits that were rescued by microglial-targeted D-NAC treatment. Previous studies showed that Mecp2-null mice had a deficit in cued fear memory, whereas Mecp2-het mice had impaired contextual fear conditioning(Stearns et al. 2007; Samaco et al. 2013). We found no deficits in contextual fear memory but instead a deficit in cued fear memory. Although these findings are incongruent with previously demonstrated deficits, we nevertheless saw impairments in fear memory. These differences in findings are likely due to variations in animal models, age, and testing paradigms. Relevant fear learning and memory circuitry have been shown to be perturbed in Mecp2-deficient models and previously have been discussed as an underlying cause of these behavioral changes(Smith et al. 2019b). However, oxidative stress and inflammation have also been implicated in the production of deficits in both contextual and cued fear learning and memory, with NAC treatment rescuing GSH, reducing 4-hydroxynonenal and nitrotyrosine, and improving both cued and contextual fear memory in EAAT3 knockout mice(Cao et al. 2012).

Patients with RTT frequently experience sleep disturbances, including night-waking and decreased sleep efficiency, with 80% reporting sleep issues at some point during their lifespan with incidence increasing with age (Amaddeo et al. 2019; Boban et al. 2016). Sleep efficiency is decreased markedly, primarily due to waking after sleep onset(Amaddeo et al. 2019). Using a standardized sleep disturbance scale, the most pathologically elevated sub scores (compared to controls) were disorders of initiating or maintaining sleep score and sleep-wake transition disorders score(Boban et al. 2016). There are currently no approved medications for sleep issues in children with Rett syndrome and therapeutic approaches such as melatonin only partially mitigate sleep dysfunction(McArthur & Budden 1998). Studies investigating sleep macro architecture in children with Rett syndrome have reported significant impairments. Polysomnographic studies in Rett syndrome have reported reduced REM and increased N3 or slow-wave-sleep (SWS) (Amaddeo et al. 2019; Zhang et al. 2023). Quantitative EEG studies specifically investigating SWS abnormalities in Rett syndrome reported reduced SWS time and fewer SWS cycles in individuals with Rett syndrome. These decrements in SWS seen in patients have specifically been correlated to certain severity markers such as seizures. Further quantitative analysis of SWS revealed an abnormally high voltage delta activity that did not undergo overnight regression as seen in typically developing children (Ammanuel et al. 2015). Few animal studies have investigated sleep structure. Animals models of RTT have shown varied findings with poor sleep continuity and increased fragmentation noted (reviewed in Zhang et al, 2020).Mouse models have revealed enhanced waking state, impaired NREM and REM dynamics and poor quality of SWS (Johnston et al. 2014). The transgenic line used in these experiments (Mecp2tm1.1Bird) more accurately models sleep impairments observed in patients (i.e. decreased REM and non-REM sleep, and sleep fragmentation or increased waking during sleep). Given the genotypic and phenotypic fidelity with Mepc2-het mice, we have a robust method for studying the pathophysiology of sleep disturbances in RTT.

REM sleep is important for brain development especially in early periods of life and facilitates formation and consolidation of certain types of memory(Ohayon et al. 2004; Rasch & Born 2013). Improvement in REM sleep with D-NAC treatment indicates that glia are key players in disordered sleep of RTT patients. Beyond RTT, the Mecp2-het model provides substantial evidence for a bidirectional relationship between sleep and inflammation. Poor, disordered sleep (including sleep deprivation and sleep fragmentation) has been shown to increase inflammatory cytokines(Villafuerte et al. 2015; Bertrand et al. 2020). However, our data as well as others indicate that altered glial activity, including inflammation, can result in impaired sleep(Krueger & Obál Jr 1993). D-NAC treatment recovered REM sleep, suggesting that REM-specific processes are affected by oxidative stress and inflammatory mechanisms.

Interestingly, D-NAC improvements were specific to REM sleep and NREM sleep parameters showed no improvement after D-NAC treatment. A possible mechanism by which this could occur is through IL-1B inhibition. IL-1B differentially regulates REM and NREM processes, and while reducing IL-1B levels improves REM, reductions in IL-1B may perturb NREM sleep. (Imeri et al. 2004; Krueger & Obál Jr 1993; Krueger & Toth 1994; Terao et al. 1998). These data highlight the need for future work to characterize microglial dysregulation and their effects on both REM and NREM sleep. It is also possible that longer treatment periods may be needed for more comprehensive improvement in sleep structure.

Neuroinflammation plays a prominent role in epileptiform activity and epileptogenesis, as demonstrated by significant perturbations in antioxidant pathways, cytokines, and chemokines in temporal lobe epilepsy(Koh 2018; Ambrogini et al. 2019). Increases in inflammatory cytokines, glutamate release, and oxidative stress conditions all likely contribute to the neuronal hyper-excitability and epileptiform activity observed in RTT mouse models (Calfa et al. 2011; Janc & Muller 2014; Gogliotti et al. 2016). These results not only provide additional evidence of the connection between neuroinflammation and epileptiform activity, but also point to a role for microglial dysfunction in epileptogenesis in RTT. Current treatments including anticonvulsants have been reported to have varying levels of efficacy(Dolce et al. 2013), with the majority of patients requiring these medications to remain seizure-free(Tarquinio et al. 2017). This novel approach may therefore provide a pathology-modifying treatment that more effectively reduces seizure burden in RTT as well as in other epileptic conditions related to inflammation and oxidative stress.

We have also replicated others’ findings that Mecp2-deficient microglia have an increase in pro-inflammatory-like phenotype as measured by TNF-α and IL-1β cytokine production(Cronk et al. 2015; Zhao et al. 2017). Mecp2-KO microglia and macrophages show an activated morphology and functionality as disease burden increases and demonstrate an increased expression of TNFα-inducible genes (as well as glucocorticoid- and hypoxia-inducible genes)(Kahanovitch et al. 2019; Cronk et al. 2015; Schafer et al. 2016). These findings are of particular interest because alterations in microglia result in altered synaptic connectivity - purported to be the direct cause of neural disruption in RTT(Maezawa & Jin 2010; Xu et al. 2014; Johnston et al. 2005). In this study, in vivo D-NAC treatment reduced proinflammatory cytokine production in isolated CD11b+ cells from Mecp2-het mice. Via NF-κB, D-NAC administration to microglia is able to shift microglia away from a pro-inflammatory-like phenotype(Kannan et al. 2012).

While these findings provide valuable information about global microglial dysfunction in RTT, regional heterogeneity of microglia likely play a role in the production of region-specific neuropathology(Tan et al. 2020). Furthermore, in Mecp2-het mice, the presence/absence of MeCP2 may also contribute to activation profile. Mecp2-knockout microglia specifically show increased responsivity to stimulation(Nance et al. 2017; Cronk et al. 2015). Future work will investigate microglial changes and the impact of D-NAC in relevant regions such as the frontal cortex and hippocampus.

Taken together, these findings illustrate that glial-mediated oxidative stress and inflammation play an important role in the production of behavioral phenotype in a Mecp2-het mouse model of RTT. A G4 PAMAM-OH nanoparticle platform can target the implicated glia and deliver NAC at a fraction of the effective dose required with free drug administration, while also reducing NAC toxicity. While we only investigated the effect of D-NAC on microglia, it is also likely that there is some degree of D-NAC uptake in activated astrocytes as well. Future work will continue to refine our understanding of the relationship between oxidative stress/immune dysfunction of various glia sub-types and behavioral phenotypes, as well as further optimization of D-NAC treatment. Although we demonstrate metabolic derangements in the hippocampus and striatum in this model, a comprehensive metabolomic assessment after D-NAC treatment was beyond the scope of this study. Future studies focused on the effect of D-NAC in lipid metabolism and acylcarnitine metabolites will provide a better understanding of the role of microglia in the propagation of these abnormalities. With no approved disease modifying therapies for RTT, our results show that these nanoparticle-delivered therapies may prove efficacious in altering the clinical course of this disorder.
